items.prompt: Why do animals need to sleep at all?

options.label: Sleep clears waste that builds up in the brain
options.feedback: While an animal is awake and its brain is busy, chemical by-products pile up around brain cells, and sleep is when the brain flushes much of that debris away.

options.label: Sleep stops the body from growing too fast
options.feedback: Growth continues and can even speed up during sleep in young animals, so sleep is not acting as a brake on growth.

options.label: Sleep lets the animal go without eating
options.feedback: A sleeping animal still burns fuel to keep its brain and organs running; sleep reduces that use somewhat but does not replace the need for food.

options.label: Sleep exists only to rest tired muscles
options.feedback: Simply lying still and awake already rests the muscles; sleep does something to the brain that ordinary awake rest does not.

items.ok_line: A nightly clean-out the brain cannot manage while it's busy being awake.
items.ko_line: Think about what piles up inside a brain that is constantly active, not about the muscles or the stomach.
items.exp_title: A nightly clean-out for the brain
items.exp_text: A brain that is awake and constantly thinking produces chemical by-products as a normal side effect of all that activity, and those by-products need to be cleared away. During sleep, the channels that carry fluid around brain cells widen and the flow through them speeds up, flushing that debris out far more effectively than happens during waking hours. That nightly clearing is one reason a brain deprived of sleep starts to struggle, however much the rest of the body gets to rest instead.

items.prompt: What is happening inside an animal's brain during the twitchy, restless phase of sleep known as REM?

options.label: The brain has almost completely shut down
options.feedback: Brain activity during this phase looks close to an awake, alert brain, which is the opposite of shutting down.

options.label: The body is simply cold and shivering
options.feedback: The twitching seen here is not shivering for warmth; it happens at any comfortable temperature and looks quite different from a shiver.

options.label: Brain activity closely resembles being awake
options.feedback: Brain waves during this phase look remarkably similar to an alert, waking brain, even though the body stays deeply asleep and mostly still.

options.label: The animal is fully awake and moving around
options.feedback: During this phase most of the body's large muscles are held in a temporary paralysis, which is exactly why the brain can be this active while the body stays still.

items.ok_line: A brain that looks awake, wrapped in a body that cannot act on it.
items.ko_line: Think about how active the brain itself is during this phase, not how still the body looks.
items.exp_title: A busy brain in a still body
items.exp_text: During REM sleep, an animal's brain produces patterns of electrical activity that closely resemble those of an awake, alert brain, even though the animal remains deeply asleep. At the same time, signals from the brain temporarily switch off most of the body's large muscles, so the twitches visible from outside are only a small leak of activity that manages to slip through. That combination, a busy brain paired with a mostly paralysed body, is what lets an animal's paws or tail flick and its eyes dart without the rest of the body acting out whatever the brain is doing.

items.prompt: How does a hibernating animal survive for months without eating anything at all?

options.label: It slowly digests its own muscle for fuel
options.feedback: A hibernating animal actually protects its muscle and loses remarkably little of it; the fuel it burns comes from somewhere else in the body.

options.label: It burns fat reserves built up beforehand
options.feedback: In the weeks before hibernating, the animal eats heavily and stores the surplus as fat, and that stored fat becomes the only fuel its slowed body needs for the entire winter.

options.label: It absorbs nutrients directly from soil while burrowed
options.feedback: Soil holds no usable nutrients an animal's body could absorb this way; whatever fuel it uses has to already be inside its own body.

options.label: Its body pauses digestion and needs nothing at all
options.feedback: The body still needs fuel to keep the heart beating and the brain minimally active, even at a much reduced rate; nothing living can run on no fuel whatsoever.

items.ok_line: A fuel tank filled before the sleep begins, and rationed carefully through it.
items.ko_line: Think about what the animal did in the weeks before it ever stopped eating.
items.exp_title: Living off a fuel tank filled in advance
items.exp_text: Before hibernating, an animal feeds heavily and converts much of that extra food into fat, building up a reserve large enough to last through the whole period of dormancy. Once hibernation begins, its metabolism drops sharply and its body draws on that stored fat for essentially all its energy, with almost no food coming in from outside. Breaking fat down for fuel also releases water as a by-product, which is part of why a hibernating animal can go so long without drinking as well as without eating.

items.prompt: How does a hibernating animal warm itself back up after weeks near-freezing, ready to rouse?

options.label: Sunlight reaching the den warms it passively
options.feedback: Most hibernation dens are sheltered from direct sunlight, and this warming happens even in dark, insulated burrows with no sun reaching them at all.

options.label: It simply waits for the outside air to warm
options.feedback: Rousing happens well before the season outside has warmed at all, and it happens repeatedly through the coldest part of winter, not just once in spring.

options.label: Its heart stops needing to pump as hard
options.feedback: The heart actually speeds up sharply during this warming process, working harder rather than needing to work less.

options.label: Special fat tissue burns fuel purely to produce heat
options.feedback: A tissue called brown fat, along with rapid shivering, generates heat directly by burning stored fuel, warming the animal's core from the inside out well before it becomes active.

items.ok_line: Heat made from the inside, not borrowed from outside.
items.ko_line: Think about a tissue whose whole job is to burn fuel purely for warmth.
items.exp_title: Heat made from the inside, not borrowed
items.exp_text: A hibernating animal cannot simply wait for outside warmth to reach a body that has dropped close to the temperature of its surroundings. Instead, it generates its own heat: a special tissue called brown fat burns fuel to produce warmth directly rather than to power movement, and this is joined by intense shivering as the body rouses. Working together, these two sources of heat can raise the animal's core temperature back toward normal from deep within, spreading outward until the whole body is ready to move again.

items.prompt: How can a wood frog survive being frozen almost solid through the winter?

options.label: A natural antifreeze in its cells stops the ice damaging them
options.feedback: As the frog begins to freeze, its body floods its cells with a concentrated sugar that keeps ice from forming inside them, even as ice spreads through the spaces between cells and around its organs.

options.label: Its blood keeps flowing even while frozen
options.feedback: As the frog freezes, its heart actually stops beating altogether and blood stops flowing entirely, only starting again once the frog thaws.

options.label: It buries itself too deep for the cold to reach
options.feedback: A wood frog typically shelters in shallow leaf litter, shallow enough that the ground around it does freeze; the frog itself is built to survive that freezing rather than avoid it.

options.label: It produces its own body heat to stay above freezing
options.feedback: The frog generates no heat of its own during this time; its body temperature is allowed to drop and match the frozen ground around it.

items.ok_line: Ice fills the spaces between cells; a natural antifreeze keeps it out of the cells themselves.
items.ko_line: Think about what protects the inside of each individual cell, not the frog's body as a whole.
items.exp_title: Ice everywhere except inside the cells
items.exp_text: As temperatures drop, a wood frog lets ice spread through the spaces between its cells and around its organs, while its liver rapidly converts stored sugar into a concentrated syrup that floods into the cells themselves. That syrup lowers the freezing point inside each cell and draws water out of it before ice can form there, so the delicate structures inside every cell stay intact even as the frog outside them turns hard and stiff. Its heart and breathing stop completely during this time, and they start up again once the frog begins to thaw.

items.prompt: How does an arctic ground squirrel keep its blood from freezing even though its body temperature drops below the normal freezing point of water?

options.label: Its blood is naturally saltier than other animals'
options.feedback: Ordinary blood salt levels lower the freezing point only slightly; something else has to explain a drop this large.

options.label: It shivers constantly to stay just above freezing
options.feedback: Constant shivering would burn through its fuel reserves far too quickly to last an entire winter; this animal's body temperature is allowed to fall, not held just above the line.

options.label: Its blood stays liquid without anything to trigger ice to form
options.feedback: Ice normally needs a tiny particle or rough surface to start forming around, and this squirrel's body is kept remarkably free of anything that could act as that starting point, so its blood can stay liquid at a temperature where it would ordinarily freeze.

options.label: Its body swaps water in the blood for oil instead
options.feedback: The squirrel's blood remains water-based throughout hibernation; nothing in its body is replaced with a different liquid.

items.ok_line: Without a seed for ice to start on, water can stay liquid below its usual freezing point.
items.ko_line: Think about what water actually needs before ice crystals can start forming in it.
items.exp_title: Liquid below the usual freezing point
items.exp_text: Water does not have to freeze the instant it reaches its normal freezing point; it needs a tiny seed, some particle or rough surface for the first ice crystals to start growing on. An arctic ground squirrel's body is kept extraordinarily clean of anything that could act as that seed, so during the coldest stretches of hibernation its blood and body fluids can drop below the temperature where ice would normally form and still stay liquid. The moment something disturbs that delicate balance, such as a rough touch or a stray particle, ice can begin forming almost instantly throughout the fluid.

items.prompt: How does a lungfish survive for months after the swamp it lives in dries up completely?

options.label: It grows temporary legs and walks to water
options.feedback: A lungfish has no ability to grow legs; it survives the dry period in place rather than travelling anywhere.

options.label: It burrows into the mud and seals itself in a cocoon
options.feedback: Before the water disappears, it digs down into the mud and coats itself in a layer of hardened mucus that keeps it from drying out, leaving only a narrow channel open to breathe through.

options.label: It simply holds its breath until the rain returns
options.feedback: Holding its breath for that long would be impossible for any animal; this species keeps breathing air throughout the dry period rather than stopping.

options.label: It converts to breathing underwater through gills alone
options.feedback: This fish actually relies on a lung to breathe air during the dry period, the opposite of switching to gill breathing.

items.ok_line: Sealed in mud, breathing through a narrow channel to the surface.
items.ko_line: Think about what the fish does to the mud around it before the water is gone.
items.exp_title: Sealed in mud, breathing through a straw
items.exp_text: As its swamp dries out, a lungfish burrows down into the softening mud and, as the mud hardens around it, secretes a layer of mucus that dries into a tough, protective cocoon holding in moisture. A narrow channel through that cocoon stays open to the surface, and because this fish also has a lung as well as gills, it can keep breathing air through that channel for the whole dry period. Its whole body slows down drastically inside the cocoon, using stored energy sparingly until rain eventually softens the ground and lets it dig free.

items.prompt: How does a hummingbird survive a cold night after burning through its fuel so fast during the day?

options.label: It migrates somewhere warmer each evening
options.feedback: This happens every single night in the same location, not as a journey somewhere else, so travel is not the explanation.

options.label: It huddles in a large group for warmth
options.feedback: Hummingbirds are solitary at rest and do not gather in groups to share warmth overnight; whatever protects them, they manage it alone.

options.label: It eats continuously through the night
options.feedback: Most hummingbirds cannot feed in the dark at all, so surviving the night has to rely on something other than continuing to eat.

options.label: It drops its body temperature and slows its heart drastically
options.feedback: Entering a state called torpor, it lets its body temperature fall a long way and its heart rate slow to a small fraction of its daytime pace, cutting its overnight fuel use enormously compared with staying fully warm.

items.ok_line: Powering the body down on purpose, rather than trying to stay fully warm all night.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the bird's own body temperature overnight, not what it does outside its body.
items.exp_text: A hummingbird's daytime metabolism runs so fast that its small store of fuel could not otherwise last through a long, cold night. Each evening it can enter a state called torpor, letting its body temperature drop steeply and its heartbeat and breathing slow right down, so the body uses only a small fraction of the fuel it would burn staying fully warm. Coming out of torpor takes real effort the following morning, as the bird must warm itself back up before it can fly at all.

items.prompt: How does a turtle resting at the bottom of a frozen pond all winter manage without surfacing to breathe air?

options.label: It absorbs enough oxygen through skin near its tail
options.feedback: Its metabolism slows so drastically in the cold that the small amount of oxygen it can take in through thin, blood-rich tissue near its tail is enough to keep it alive without ever needing a lungful of air.

options.label: It stores a large reserve of air under its shell
options.feedback: There is no air pocket held under a turtle's shell of this kind; whatever oxygen it uses through the winter has to come from the water around it.

options.label: It simply stops needing oxygen for the whole winter
options.feedback: Every living cell still needs some oxygen to keep functioning, even at a much reduced rate; nothing about this turtle's body can do without any at all.

options.label: It breaks through the ice regularly to breathe
options.feedback: Ice covering the pond stays intact through the cold months, and this turtle survives the whole stretch without breaking through it even once.

items.ok_line: A trickle of oxygen through the skin, matched to a body slowed right down.
items.ko_line: Think about how little oxygen a body needs once its whole metabolism has slowed right down.
items.exp_text: Once the water turns too cold for a turtle to stay active, its whole metabolism slows dramatically, and the amount of oxygen its body needs drops along with it. Tissue near its tail, thin and richly supplied with blood vessels, can pull a small amount of dissolved oxygen directly out of the surrounding water and pass it into the bloodstream. That trickle of oxygen, tiny as it is, turns out to be exactly enough to keep a turtle's slowed body running until the ice above it finally breaks up.

items.prompt: How do some fish keep swimming in water cold enough that their blood should freeze solid?

options.label: Their blood is naturally warmer than the water
options.feedback: These fish have no way to keep their blood warmer than the surrounding water; their body temperature simply matches the cold water around them.

options.label: They avoid the coldest water entirely
options.feedback: Some of these fish live permanently among the coldest waters on the planet, so avoiding the cold cannot be what protects them.

options.label: Special proteins in their blood stop ice crystals growing
options.feedback: These proteins attach directly to the tiny ice crystals that start to form and physically block them from growing any larger, so the blood can carry a scattering of harmless, stalled ice specks instead of freezing solid.

options.label: Their blood contains almost no water at all
options.feedback: Their blood is still mostly water, the same as any other fish; what differs is a special protein dissolved in it, not the water content itself.

items.ok_line: Ice crystals still start to form; the protein just refuses to let them grow.
items.ko_line: Think about a substance dissolved in the blood that could act directly on tiny ice crystals.
items.exp_title: Proteins that stop ice in its tracks
items.exp_text: In icy seas, stray ice crystals can drift into a fish's bloodstream and, left alone, would keep growing until the blood froze solid. Certain fish carry specialised proteins in their blood that bind directly onto the surface of any tiny ice crystal that begins to form, physically blocking more water molecules from joining and making the crystal grow any further. Held at that harmless, stalled size, the ice crystals drift through the bloodstream doing no damage at all, letting the fish keep swimming through water that would otherwise freeze it solid.
